title: Little Professor

source.quote: I relied more on intuition, instant impressions.

setting: Tuesday, 6:30pm. Dinner. Mike, three years old, has been pushing the same four pieces of broccoli around his plate for ten minutes. Mom is out tonight.

L1.line: Mommy said I don't have to eat broccoli when she's not here.
cues: checks Dad's face right after saying it
timed for the one night no one can check with Mom
L1.question: Mike isn't crying and he isn't openly refusing. What's actually running underneath this line?

options.text: Free Child - he's just saying what he feels
options.feedback: Free Child would look more like a flat refusal or a meltdown over the broccoli itself; this isn't an outburst, it's a claim timed for exactly the moment no one can check it.

options.text: The Little Professor - intuitive, strategic thinking, not feeling
options.feedback: Right. Berne's "Professor" (A1, the Adult in the Child) is the child's intuitive problem-solving power - it doesn't reason like a grown-up, but it's sharp, reads the room, and just worked out that an unverifiable claim made on Mom's night out might get the broccoli waived.

options.text: He's lying, full stop, there's nothing more to it
options.feedback: It is an invented claim - but calling it just "lying" misses what's interesting: a three-year-old timed it, delivered it calmly, and watched for your reaction. That's strategy, which is exactly what the Little Professor names.

options.text: Adult - he's doing real cost-benefit reasoning
options.feedback: It has the shape of strategy, but it isn't grown-up reasoning with real information - it's childhood intuition, quick and clever but not the reality-tested Adult; TA keeps this filed as Child content (the Little Professor), not Adult.

L1.lesson: The common confusion here is that the Child ego-state is pure feeling - but Berne's second-order model puts real thinking inside it too: intuitive, fast, unschooled, but thinking all the same. Mike isn't melting down. He's experimenting.

L2.intro: You know Mom didn't say any such thing. This is the first move of something, not the whole game yet. What do you do?

beats.line: Mommy said. Really! She said it this morning.
cues: adds a small detail to make it sound more real

options.text: Okay, fine, you don't have to eat it tonight.
options.outcome: Mike's eyes light up - just for a flash - before he goes back to his cartoon voice: "Okay!" The broccoli goes in the bin. Lesson filed away: that line works.
options.lesson: Taking the bait lets the Little Professor's hypothesis get confirmed - next week it won't be broccoli, it'll be bedtime, or screen time, or Mom's name used again. The game just got its first successful run.

options.text: Really? That doesn't sound like Mom. Let's call her and ask.
options.outcome: Mike's face flickers - caught - then he laughs and says "okay, okay, no" and eats a piece of broccoli, grinning. No fight, no lecture.
options.lesson: Checking the claim against reality from Adult, without anger, answers the Little Professor's experiment on its own terms: the hypothesis doesn't survive contact with a simple reality check, so the game never gets a chance to form.

options.text: That's a lie, Mike, and lying is wrong.
options.outcome: Mike's lip trembles and he goes quiet, pushing the broccoli further away. The claim doesn't get repeated tonight - but it comes back, crying, three nights later.
options.lesson: This stops tonight's move, but a moral verdict from Controlling Parent teaches Mike to fear getting caught, not that the claim doesn't hold up - the Little Professor just adjusts its strategy for next time instead of retiring it.

options.text: Just eat two more pieces and you can be done.
options.outcome: Mike considers, then eats two pieces without further comment. Reasonable tonight, though the claim about Mom is never actually addressed.
options.lesson: A fair, concrete trade resolves tonight's dinner, but it sidesteps the actual move Mike made - the invented claim is left unchecked, free to be tried again somewhere else.

fields.label: Draw the vectors for Mike's claim, and for the father's best response.

Berne called catching a game early "in statu nascendi" - literally, "while it's still being born," before it has a chance to fully form. In under 60 words: which response here actually does that, and why?

echo.setting: 24 hours later: Raj's own coworker floats a confident-sounding claim about what "legal already approved" for a shortcut.
echo.line: Legal already signed off on this, I checked yesterday.
echo.shape: same reality-check-before-it-forms shape as the best L2 move
